theme: Smells & statistics: describing the world · 냄새와 통계, 세상을 표현하는 법

tracks.title: How do we describe smells?
tracks.note: Neil과 Georgie가 영어로 냄새를 어떻게 표현하는지 이야기해요. 비 온 뒤 땅 냄새는 petrichor, 헌책 냄새는 vellichor! 영어에는 냄새 '자체'를 묘사하는 단어가 적고, 보통 'smells like ~'로 비교해서 말한대요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I'm Neil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And I'm Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: In English, there are many ways to describe smells.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Poet Michael Rosen wanted to find words describing bad smells, and asked listeners of his BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth for some suggestions.

transcript.speaker: Michael Rosen
transcript.text: Fusty, reeking, toiking, honking, humming, funky…

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Smells are everywhere, whether they're bad smells like rotten eggs and sweaty feet, or pleasant ones like lavender and freshly baked bread.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: What smells do you especially like or dislike, Georgie?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, I really enjoy the smell of leather, but something I really love is the smell of rain, which has a name.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Do you know it, Neil?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Erm, I don't think I do actually.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It's called petrichor.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It's that smell of the ground just after it's rained.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Mmm.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Neil, what about you?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Which smells do you like?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, I don't think you can beat the smell of a freshly opened packet of ground coffee.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Ooh, that's a good one.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: In this episode, we'll be learning the language of smells using some useful new words and phrases.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And remember, you can find all the vocabulary plus a quiz and worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: But first, I have a question for you, Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: One smell many people love is the smell of old books and the sentimental feeling it gives them for second-hand bookshops.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: In fact, there's even a word for it, but what is it?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is it: a) vellichor, b) petrichor, or c) nidor?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, we already know that petrichor is the smell of the ground after rain.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I'm going to go with a) vellichor.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, we'll find out at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Listening to Michael Rosen's list – funky, reeking, humming and the rest – you might think English is good at describing smells, but in fact, all those words really mean is bad smelling.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: In English, we often describe smells by comparing them to other objects.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: For example, something nice might smell like a rose, while something bad might smell like rotten eggs, but there are few words to describe the actual smell itself.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Oxford University psychologist Asifa Majid has researched the subject of smell extensively.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Here, she tells Michael Rosen a little of what she's found out on BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: So, if we think about things like stinky or fragrant, they're definitely telling us that something is good or bad.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: But unlike colour terms, it doesn't really seem to be about the object it's describing.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: It seems to be a subjective thing.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: I could say, "Oh this perfume you think is really fragrant, I think is stinky," and both can be true.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Describing smell is not like describing other senses.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I might think a perfume is stinky, an adjective meaning bad smelling, while Neil might find the same perfume fragrant, meaning pleasant smelling.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Both can be true.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The point is that neither stinky nor fragrant say anything specific about the perfume's actual smell.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: With our sense of taste, it's different.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Words like spicy, sweet or salty create a common idea that we can all agree on, but that's not the case for smells.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Asifa thinks this is because, unlike tastes and colours, smell words are subjective – they're based on personal opinions and feelings rather than objective truth.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: This might explain why our attitude to talking about smells is so different.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Here's Asifa again, sharing some examples of how we talk about smells with BBC Radio 4.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: So, if we compare how often people talk about visual things, or auditory things, or tastes or smells, what we find is we talk a lot about what we see and very rarely about what we smell.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: Young children in the UK are often interested in the sense of smell and they'll remark on it, and the parent will shut it down.

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: They'll say, "That's disgusting!

transcript.speaker: Asifa Majid
transcript.text: Put it down."

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Asifa's research shows that, here in the UK at least, people talk about visual or auditory things much more than they talk about smells.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The adjective visual means related to seeing, and auditory means related to hearing.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The adjective for things related to smelling is olfactory.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Maybe this is because of how we're raised by our parents.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: When children start talking about smells, especially unpleasant ones, parents often react by shutting the conversation down.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The phrase to shut something down means to stop it.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Along with other European languages, English doesn't have much vocabulary dedicated to the different qualities of actual smells.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: There are many ways of talking about smells, especially unpleasant ones, but only a few words which describe actual smells themselves.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A good example of a word which does this is musty – a damp, stale smell you might find in an old bookshop.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And Neil, that reminds me of your question.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I asked you what the word is, which means the smell of old books.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I said it was vellichor.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, Georgie, you are absolutely right.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yay!

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Petrichor, as you said earlier, is the smell of the earth after rain.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And nidor is the smell of cooking meat and fat.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It's time for a recap of the vocabulary we've learned.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The adjective stinky means foul smelling, while the adjective fragrant means pleasant smelling.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Subjective things are based on your own personal opinions and feelings rather than objective facts.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The adjective visual describes things related to seeing, while auditory means related to hearing.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Things related to smelling are called olfactory.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And finally, the phrasal verb to shut something down means to stop it.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but there's still time to head over to our website, bbclearningenglish.com, for a quiz and worksheet containing all the vocabulary we've discussed.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: See you again soon!

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But for now, it's goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Goodbye!

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'fragrant', 'subjective', 'shut down'이 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: What is the word for the smell of old books? a) vellichor, b) petrichor, c) nidor
quiz.answer: a) vellichor. Georgie가 맞혔어요! petrichor는 비 온 뒤 땅 냄새, nidor는 고기와 기름을 요리하는 냄새예요.

sentences.text: It's that smell of the ground just after it's rained.
sentences.ko: 비가 온 직후 땅에서 나는 그 냄새예요.

sentences.text: Well, I don't think you can beat the smell of a freshly opened packet of ground coffee.
sentences.ko: 갓 뜯은 원두커피 냄새를 이길 건 없는 것 같아요.

sentences.text: Describing smell is not like describing other senses.
sentences.ko: 냄새를 묘사하는 건 다른 감각을 묘사하는 것과 달라요.

sentences.text: Maybe this is because of how we're raised by our parents.
sentences.ko: 어쩌면 부모님이 우리를 키우는 방식 때문일지도 몰라요.

sentences.text: The phrase to shut something down means to stop it.
sentences.ko: 'shut something down'이라는 표현은 그걸 멈추게 한다는 뜻이에요.

reading.title: America does not produce world-beating statistics. Who does?
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 전 세계적으로 공식 통계 조사 응답률이 무너지고(미국 소비지출 조사 응답률 60%→40% 미만), 예산 삭감과 정치 개입까지 겹쳐 '통계 위기'가 왔어요. Economist는 네 가지 기준(자주 발표하는가, 정치적으로 독립적인가, 정확한가, 변화에 적응하는가)으로 최고의 통계 기관을 찾았어요. 미국·영국은 탈락, 인구등록부(population register)를 가진 네덜란드·노르웨이·스위스와 캐나다가 상위권, 그중 혁신성에서 네덜란드가 1등. 검사실에서 매일 데이터의 정확도를 다루는 입장에서 공감할 만한 글이에요.
excerpt: Everyone should worry about the stats-pocalypse, not least because policy drawn up using junk statistics risks being junk itself. Central banks need reliable employment data to set interest rates.
It is not enough to produce statistics frequently and without fear or favour. A good system also needs to consistently get the numbers right.
reading.tip: 'not least because ~'는 '특히 ~ 때문에'라는 뜻으로 중요한 이유를 강조할 때 써요. 'without fear or favour'는 '두려움도 편애도 없이 = 공정하게'라는 관용구. 'junk statistics risks being junk itself'처럼 같은 단어를 반복해 재치 있게 말하는 게 Economist 스타일이에요.

vocab.example: Neil might find the same perfume fragrant.
Smell words are subjective – they're based on personal opinions.
When children talk about smells, parents often shut the conversation down.
Response rates to official surveys have collapsed globally.
Central banks need reliable employment data to set interest rates.
Tax records can provide a much more granular picture.
Statistical offices must be beyond suspicion.

writing.prompt: Write 3–5 sentences in English about why accurate data matters in your work at the clinical lab.
writing.question: What happens if a lab result is wrong? How do you make sure your numbers are reliable?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: In my lab, accurate results are important because ... / If a result is wrong, ... / We check ... to make sure the data is reliable.

speaking.prompt: In one minute, describe a smell you love and a smell you hate. Why do you feel that way?
phrases: I really love the smell of ...
I can't stand the smell of ... It smells like ...
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: Name three smells you like, in three short sentences (e.g. I like the smell of coffee.).
